detected_by: git status --porcelain, run before staging this cycle's commit per the shared-checkout discipline: it listed 7 modified files this cycle never touched, plus an untracked docs/retro/events/sd29-e9-version.jsonl naming the sibling actor.
impact: This cycle's full verify.sh gate cannot be attributed to this cycle's diff alone -- it measures a working tree that also contains sibling cycle sd29-e9-version's in-flight version-numbering changes (.github/workflows/publish-tester-release.yml, apps/desktop/package.json, apps/desktop/src-tauri/{Cargo.toml,Cargo.lock,tauri.conf.json}, and two buildVersionTriple.test.ts files). A red stage would be ambiguous between the two cycles by construction; a green one certifies the mixture, not either card. AGENTS.md 'One writer per tree' makes this a stop-and-report condition.
resolution: This cycle's commit was taken and is safe: explicit disjoint paths only (three SD-29 docs plus its own retro shard), no git add -A, no git stash, no sibling file staged, reverted or stashed. The gate result is recorded in progress.md with this contamination named rather than reported as a clean measurement. Not escalated to a halt: this card adds no code path, so it cannot itself have caused any stage failure, and idling would stall the bundle under unattended mode.
summary: Sibling Epic 9 held uncommitted work in the shared checkout during this cycle's gate; result attribution recorded as mixed.

detected_by: Reading the exit code as a number instead of as pass/fail: the runner wrote 143, and 143 = 128+15 = SIGTERM, not a verify.sh verdict. The log corroborated it -- it ended mid-'root-full' with no FAIL line and no SUMMARY block, i.e. the process was terminated, not concluded.
impact: A full verify.sh run was killed ~10 minutes in, during root-full's ~490-binary build. The danger was not the lost run but the misreading available: a non-zero exit code with four PASS stages already printed reads exactly like a failing gate, and recording 143 as 'gate red' would have manufactured a phantom blocker for a docs-only cycle that touches no code path. Symmetrically, the harness's own task notification for the wrapper reported 'completed (exit code 0)' -- the WRAPPER's status, not verify.sh's -- so the two available summaries pointed in opposite directions and neither was the gate's verdict.
resolution: Cause was self-inflicted and not environmental: the gate was launched via a backgrounded Bash call carrying timeout=600000, and the harness killed the process group at that 10-minute deadline. verify.sh under contention takes far longer than any harness timeout should be asked to hold. Relaunched with setsid+nohup+disown and stdio detached to /dev/null so the run outlives the harness's task lifecycle entirely, and the exit code is read from a file the runner writes after assigning code=$? directly. Build cache was warm (13G target dir survived), so the re-run resumed cheaply.
summary: verify.sh exit 143 was a harness-timeout SIGTERM, not a gate failure; relaunched detached. Neither the raw exit code nor the harness's task summary is the gate's verdict.

detected_by: pgrep -af immediately after running the kill: the listing showed sibling cycle sd29-e9-version's live gate (pid 1362638, 'bash ./scripts/verify.sh --show-actuals') still in the process table, which is the only reason the near-miss was noticed at all rather than discovered later as an unexplained dead gate.
impact: NEAR-MISS, no damage. To stop this cycle's own gate I ran pkill -9 -f 'scripts/verify.sh' -- a pattern match, not a PID. Epic 9 was concurrently running './scripts/verify.sh --show-actuals' in the same shared checkout, whose command line contains that exact substring, so the pattern was capable of killing a sibling's ~45-minute gate mid-root-full. Had it landed, Epic 9 would have seen a gate die with no cause in its own log and no notification -- indistinguishable from the harness-timeout SIGTERM this same cycle had already been fooled by once.
resolution: Both processes survived; verified by ps -p on each PID before proceeding. This cycle's gate was then killed by explicit PID (kill -9 1347807) and re-verified, and the sibling's was re-confirmed alive. Rule for shared checkouts: never pkill -f on a pattern that names a shared tool -- resolve to a PID first (pgrep -af, read the listing, kill by number), because on a shared checkout every agent's gate has the same command line by construction. The pattern that feels specific to your own process is specific to the tool, which everyone runs.
summary: Broad pkill -f 'scripts/verify.sh' could have killed a sibling's live gate; caught by ps, killed by PID instead.
